_comment: Question bank for the Complexity Quiz (site/pages/lc-complexity-quiz.html).
Each entry shows a Python snippet and asks for its time and space complexity.
Fields:
id         unique slug; the quiz keys its per-question state off it
lc         LeetCode number, or null for a pure algorithm / Python drill
title      required only when lc is null — otherwise README.md supplies it
difficulty required only when lc is null — otherwise README.md supplies it
topic      the bucket shown in the score breakdown and the topic filter
pack       optional: "essentials" puts it in the opt-in Interview essentials
set (the page's Question set dropdown, or ?set=essentials); omitted
means "classic", the default set. A problem lives in one set only.
vars       what each symbol in the answer means; shown above the inputs
note       the ground rule for this question (what counts as space, etc.)
code       the snippet, one array element per line
time/space the canonical answer
accept     other answers graded correct — for genuinely debatable ones only
cost       what sets each bound: { time: { lines, why }, space: { lines, why } }.
`lines` are 1-based indexes into `code` — the loop header, call or
allocation the bound comes from — and are highlighted in the snippet
once the answer is checked ([] when nothing notable allocates).
`why` is one plain sentence starting from those lines.
why        optional: the one takeaway the two cost reasons do not already say
trap       the wrong answer people actually give, and why it is wrong
site/build-quiz.js validates every entry (unique id, README-known lc, parseable
answers, cost lines inside the snippet) and fails the build rather than shipping
a question nobody can score.
The 繁體中文 text lives in data/complexity_quiz.zh.json, keyed by id. Editing an
English explanation means editing its translation too; the build fails on a
question with no translation.

time.why: `for i, x` makes one pass; each `in seen` check is an average `O(1)` hash lookup.

space.why: `seen[x] = i` can store every one of the n values before a match is found.

questions.trap: `target - x in seen` is a hash lookup, not a scan, so the loop stays linear. A nested-loop brute force is what costs `O(n^2)`.

time.why: `for p in prices` is a single pass with `O(1)` work per price.

space.why: Only two scalars, `cheapest` and `profit`, are kept; nothing grows with n.

time.why: Each pass of `while lo <= hi` halves the window, so it runs about `log n` times.

space.why: The state is just `lo`, `hi` and `mid`: three integers.

questions.title: Recursive binary search — with slicing

time.why: Each slice copies the kept half: n/2 + n/4 + … sums to `O(n)`, swamping the `log n` comparisons.

space.why: The slices still alive down the recursion path add up to n/2 + n/4 + … = `O(n)`.

questions.why: Pass `lo`/`hi` indices instead of slices to get the real `O(log n)` time and `O(1)` space.
questions.trap: It looks like textbook `O(log n)` / `O(1)` binary search. In Python, *slicing copies*, which is the most common way a correct algorithm loses its complexity.

questions.note: Ignore the space held by the result list.
code: while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo + 1]:

time.why: `for i` runs n times and each `while lo < hi` sweep is `O(n)`, so `O(n^2)`, which dominates the sort.

space.why: `nums.sort()` is Timsort, which can need up to n/2 extra slots; the pointers are `O(1)`.

questions.trap: The inner `while` inside `else` looks like a third nesting level, but `lo` and `hi` only move toward each other, so each `i` is still one linear sweep.

code: if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:

time.why: `for ch in s` visits each character once; each push or pop is `O(1)`.

space.why: `stack.append(ch)` can hold every character, e.g. for an all-opening string like `"(((("`.

time.why: `while head` visits each node once and rewires one pointer per step.

space.why: Pointers are rewired in place with three references, whatever the list length.

questions.trap: The equally common recursive version is `O(n)` space: one stack frame per node.

time.why: Once both are in the cycle, `fast` gains one node per step, so they meet within `O(n)` steps.

space.why: Two pointers, `slow` and `fast`, are the entire state.

questions.trap: A `seen = set()` solution is also `O(n)` time but `O(n)` space. Floyd's tortoise and hare is what buys constant space.

questions.vars: n, m = lengths of the two lists

time.why: `while l1 and l2` takes one node per step, and line 9 attaches the leftover in `O(1)`: at most n + m steps.

space.why: Existing nodes are spliced in place; only the `dummy` head is allocated.

time.why: `for i in range(1, len(nums))` is one pass with `O(1)` work per element.

space.why: Only `best` and `cur` are kept; `range` is lazy and copies nothing.

questions.why: Kadane's algorithm is a 1-D DP whose table collapses to one rolling value.
questions.trap: Writing the loop as `for x in nums[1:]` would quietly cost `O(n)` space, because the slice copies the array.

questions.vars: n = len(s), k = size of the character set
code: if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:

time.why: `right` advances once per character and `left` only jumps forward, so it is one pass.

space.why: `seen[ch] = right` keeps one entry per distinct character: at most k, and at most n.

questions.trap: The window never re-scans: `left` jumps straight past the duplicate. Shrinking one step at a time is still `O(n)` amortised; only restarting the scan is `O(n^2)`.

code: if 0 <= i < m and 0 <= j < n and grid[i][j] == "1":

time.why: The double loop touches all m·n cells, and `grid[i][j] = "0"` ensures each cell is sunk at most once.

space.why: The recursive `sink` calls can nest once per land cell; a snake-shaped island makes the stack `O(m * n)` deep.

questions.trap: Answering `O(1)` space because the grid is modified in place misses the call stack. The usual follow-up, a 10^6-cell grid, is asking for iterative BFS.

code: q = deque((i, j) for i in range(m) for j in range(n) if grid[i][j] == 2)
fresh = sum(row.count(1) for row in grid)
if 0 <= x < m and 0 <= y < n and grid[x][y] == 1:

time.why: The setup scans every cell, and each cell is enqueued and popped at most once with 4 neighbour checks.

space.why: The `deque` can hold most of the grid, e.g. when nearly every orange starts rotten.

questions.trap: The `for _ in range(len(q))` loop is the level marker, not extra work: it splits the same `O(m * n)` dequeues into minutes.

code: q = deque(c for c in range(numCourses) if indeg[c] == 0)

time.why: Each prerequisite is read once to build the graph, and Kahn's loop pops each course once and walks each edge once.

space.why: The adjacency list holds V lists and E entries; `indeg` and the queue add `O(V)`.

questions.trap: The nested `for nxt in graph[c]` is not a second factor of V. Summed over all courses it touches each edge exactly once, which is the E term.

questions.vars: n = number of nodes, h = tree height

time.why: Each node makes the two recursive calls exactly once, so n calls of `O(1)` work.

space.why: Recursion keeps one frame per level of the current path: h frames.

questions.why: h is `O(log n)` for a balanced tree and `O(n)` for a skewed one.
questions.trap: `O(log n)` space only holds if the tree is balanced, which the problem never promises. Say `O(h)`, then say what h is in the worst case.

code: level = [kid for node in level for kid in (node.left, node.right) if kid]

time.why: Each node is placed into exactly one `level` list and read once, so `O(n)` total.

space.why: The frontier `level` can hold the widest level, about n/2 nodes in a complete tree.

questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = the k asked for
code: return [val for cnt, val in heap]

time.why: Up to n distinct values each do a `heappush`/`heappop` on a heap capped at k, so `log k` apiece.

space.why: `Counter(nums)` can hold n distinct values, more than the k-sized heap.

questions.why: Counting is `O(n)` and is dominated by the heap loop.
questions.trap: Capping the heap at k is the point, as in `heapq.nlargest(k, freq, key=freq.get)`. Pushing every value first and popping k is `O(n log n)`.

questions.vars: n = total nodes across all lists, k = len(lists)
code: heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]

time.why: Every node is popped once and pushed once, and the heap holds at most k entries, so each operation is `log k`.

space.why: The heap holds at most one node per list: k entries.

questions.trap: Merging the lists one after another into a growing result is `O(n * k)`. The heap is what turns that k factor into `log k`.

questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = the k asked for

time.why: `for x in nums` does n pushes (and pops) on a heap that never exceeds k + 1, so `log k` each.

space.why: `heappush` grows the min-heap to k elements, and the pop keeps it there.

questions.trap: Quickselect does the same job in `O(n)` average time and `O(1)` extra space. That is the follow-up this question is fishing for.

questions.note: Count the recursion and scratch state only — the `res` list is the output.

time.why: `backtrack` reaches n! leaves, and `nums[:]` copies n elements at each one.

space.why: The recursion is n frames deep; the swaps mutate `nums` in place, so nothing else is stored.

questions.trap: `O(n!)` time undercounts: emitting a permutation is not free, because the `nums[:]` copy is `O(n)`.

questions.note: Here the output counts — `res` is the only thing that grows.

time.why: `res` doubles each of the n rounds to 2^n subsets, and `cur + [x]` copies each one, averaging n/2 elements.

space.why: The 2^n subsets built by `cur + [x]` hold about n/2 elements each, so `O(n * 2^n)` in total.

questions.trap: `O(2^n)` counts the subsets but not their contents. Any problem that emits variable-length outputs needs the length factor.

code: return -1 if dp[amount] == float("inf") else dp[amount]

time.why: `for a` fills `a` cells and `for c in coins` tries all n coins for each, so `n * a`.

space.why: `dp` has one cell per amount from 0 to `a`.

questions.trap: This is pseudo-polynomial: `a` is the input's *value*, not its length, so one more digit in `amount` multiplies the work by 10.

time.why: `for _ in range(n - 1)` runs n - 1 times with one `O(1)` addition each.

space.why: Only `a` and `b` are kept: the two values the recurrence reads.

questions.trap: Treating the big-integer additions as `O(1)` is the standard simplification and the answer interviewers want, though the numbers do grow to about n bits.

time.why: Each call branches into `fib(n - 1)` and `fib(n - 2)`, giving about 2^n calls (tightly, φ^n).

space.why: The calls run depth-first, so only one root-to-leaf path is live: n frames.

questions.trap: `O(2^n)` space confuses the size of the recursion tree with the depth of the stack. The calls never coexist.

code: prev, cur = cur, max(cur, prev + x)

time.why: `for x in nums` is one pass with `O(1)` work per house.

space.why: The recurrence looks back only two cells, so `prev` and `cur` replace the table.

questions.vars: m, n = the two string lengths

time.why: `for i` × `for j` fills each of the m·n cells once with `O(1)` work.

space.why: `dp` is an (m+1) × (n+1) table.

questions.trap: Keeping only the previous row drops space to `O(n)`, since each cell reads only the row above and its left neighbour. Worth saying out loud.

time.why: `for j in range(i)` runs 0 + 1 + … + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 times in total.

space.why: `dp` stores one value per index.

questions.trap: The inner loop being short for small i does not save an order: the triangular sum is still quadratic.

time.why: `for x in nums` does one `bisect_left` over at most n tails, so `log n` each.

space.why: `tails.append(x)` can grow the list to n entries for an increasing input.

questions.trap: `tails` is not the increasing subsequence itself; only its length is meaningful.

time.why: `for _` × `for j` still does one unit of work per grid cell: m·n.

space.why: Only one row of n values is stored and updated in place.

questions.why: Each cell needs the value above (old `row[j]`) and to its left (new `row[j-1]`), which is why one row suffices.
questions.trap: `O(m * n)` space is right for the 2-D table, not this rolling one. Spotting that the table collapses to a row is exactly the follow-up.

time.why: Each step moves `lo` or `hi` inward, so `while lo < hi` runs at most n times.

space.why: Only four scalars are kept: `lmax`, `rmax`, `total` and the pointers.

questions.trap: The prefix/suffix-max version is also `O(n)` time but `O(n)` space. The two-pointer trick is precisely what removes those arrays.

time.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner `while` pops at most n times in total.

space.why: `stack.append(i)` can hold every index, e.g. for strictly decreasing temperatures.

questions.trap: A loop inside a loop is not automatically `O(n^2)`. Count total pushes and pops, not the shape of the nesting.

questions.vars: n = items currently on the stack
questions.note: Time is for a single push / pop / getMin call.
code: cur_min = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val

time.why: `min(...)` compares two values and `self.stack[-1][1]` is a peek, so every call is `O(1)`.

space.why: `self.stack.append((val, cur_min))` stores one pair per item.

questions.why: Each entry caches the minimum of everything below it, paid for with a second value per element.
questions.trap: `min(...)` here compares two values, not the whole stack. Reading it as a scan is what makes people answer `O(n)`.

questions.note: Time is for a single get / put call.

time.why: `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` relink one node in a linked list, alongside an `O(1)` hash lookup.

space.why: `self.cache[key] = value` adds entries, and the eviction keeps the map at most c entries.

questions.why: OrderedDict is a hash map over a doubly linked list.
questions.trap: `move_to_end` sounds like it shifts elements, but it relinks one node. That is why the hash-map-plus-linked-list design is the expected answer.

questions.note: Time is for a single insert / search call.

time.why: `for ch in word` does one dict hop per character, regardless of how many words are stored.

space.why: `node.setdefault(ch, {})` can create one new node per character: L at most.

questions.why: That independence from the word count is the whole reason to build a trie.
questions.trap: Neither bound depends on how many words are stored, so no `n` belongs in either answer.

questions.vars: n = number of nodes (the matrix is n x n)
code: if isConnected[i][j] and j not in seen:

time.why: Each node is visited once, and `for j in range(n)` scans its whole matrix row: n rows × n entries.

space.why: `seen` holds up to n nodes, and the recursive `dfs(j)` can go n frames deep.

questions.trap: This is the `O(V + E)` DFS bound in disguise: an adjacency *matrix* makes the scan cost n^2 whether or not the edges exist.

code: for u, v, w in times:
return max(dist.values()) if len(dist) == n else -1

time.why: `heappush` runs at most once per edge, so up to E pushes and pops at `log E` = `O(log V)` each.

space.why: `graph` holds E edges, `dist` V nodes, and the lazy heap up to E entries.

questions.why: For a simple graph E ≤ V^2, so `log E` ≤ `2 log V`.
questions.trap: The `if u in dist: continue` line is what makes this correct without decrease-key: stale heap entries are let in and skipped on the way out.

time.why: Each pass of `while lo <= hi` keeps one half and discards the other, so about `log n` rounds.

space.why: The state is just `lo`, `hi` and `mid`.

questions.why: The extra branching only decides *which* half to keep.
questions.trap: With duplicates allowed (LC 81), `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` can no longer tell the halves apart, and the worst case degrades to `O(n)`.

code: return sum((p + speed - 1) // speed for p in piles)

time.why: `while lo < hi` tries `log m` speeds, and each `hours(mid)` sums over all n piles.

space.why: The generator inside `sum` does not build a list, so only a few integers are kept.

questions.why: This is binary search on the *answer*, not on the array.
questions.trap: The log factor is over the value range m, not the array length n. The two are unrelated, and mixing them up is the classic slip here.

questions.vars: n = len(strs), k = length of the longest word

time.why: `sorted(s)` costs `k log k` per word and runs once for each of the n words.

space.why: `groups` stores every word plus a k-length tuple key: `O(n * k)` characters.

questions.trap: The k factor is easy to drop. A 26-count tuple as the key instead of `sorted(s)` brings time down to `O(n * k)`.

time.why: The two `sorted` calls cost `n log n` each and dominate the linear `==`.

space.why: `sorted` builds a new list of n characters for each string.

questions.trap: A one-liner is not automatically `O(n)`: `sorted` on a string returns a list, and both the sort and that list cost. `Counter(s) == Counter(t)` is the `O(n)` alternative.

questions.note: The returned list is the output; do not count it as auxiliary space.

time.why: The prefix loop and the suffix loop each run n times, one after the other: `O(n) + O(n)`.

space.why: Prefix products are staged in the output `res`, and the suffix product is the single variable `right`.

questions.trap: Two loops in a row add, they do not multiply: `O(n) + O(n)` is `O(n)`.

questions.vars: m, n = the two filled lengths

time.why: `while j >= 0` writes one slot per step, and each of the m + n values is written at most once.

space.why: Values are written in place into `nums1` from the back; only three indices are kept.

questions.why: Filling from the back means nothing is ever shifted.
questions.trap: Merging forwards needs either a copy (`O(m + n)` space) or a shift per insert (`O(m * n)` time). Writing backwards avoids both.

time.why: `for x in nums` touches each element once, and `out ^= x` is O(1).

space.why: One integer accumulator, whatever the size of `nums`.

questions.why: XOR is associative and self-cancelling, so every pair annihilates and only the loner survives.
questions.trap: The set-based solution is O(n) space. The problem exists to see whether you find the O(1)-space XOR.

questions.vars: n = the integer, b = its bit width (32 here)

time.why: `n &= n - 1` clears one set bit per pass, so the `while` runs popcount ≤ `b` = 32 times.

space.why: Just `count` and the shrinking `n`.

questions.why: For a fixed-width word that is a constant; stated over the word width it is `O(b)`, and `b = log n`.
questions.trap: O(n) treats the integer's *value* as the input size. On a 32-bit word every bit trick is O(1); the general answer is O(b).

code: for lo, hi in ((i, i), (i, i + 1)):
while lo >= 0 and hi < len(s) and s[lo] == s[hi]:

time.why: `n` centres (`for i`), each `while` expanding up to `n` characters → `n²`.

space.why: `best = s[lo + 1:hi]` copies up to `n` characters; keep two indices instead and it drops to `O(1)`.

questions.trap: The two-entry tuple loop (odd and even centres) is a constant factor of 2, not a third `n`.

questions.vars: n = len(points), k = the k asked for
code: heapq.heappush(heap, (-(x * x + y * y), x, y))
return [[x, y] for _, x, y in heap]

time.why: `n` points, each `heappush` / `heappop` on a heap capped at `k` → `log k` apiece.

space.why: The heap never holds more than `k + 1` entries.

questions.why: A bounded max-heap keeps only the best `k` seen so far, so the log is over `k`, not `n`.
questions.trap: Sorting all the points is O(n log n), worse whenever k ≪ n — exactly the case the problem is built around.

time.why: `intervals.sort()` is `n log n`; the merge loop after it is a single linear pass.

space.why: Timsort needs up to `n/2` slots of scratch memory; `out` is the returned answer.

questions.trap: Almost every interval problem is O(n log n) for this reason: the sort, not the sweep, sets the bound.

time.why: `sort()` is `n log n`, then `n` heap pushes/replaces at `log n` each — the same order.

space.why: `heappush` adds one end time per concurrently open room, up to `n`.

questions.trap: `rooms[0]` is a peek at the heap root — the earliest-ending meeting — so it is O(1), not a scan.

code: while i < len(left) and j < len(right):

time.why: Two recursive halves plus a linear merge: `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)` → `log n` levels × `n` work.

space.why: The slices `nums[:mid]` / `nums[mid:]` and the merged `out` hold `O(n)` at once; the stack is only `log n` deep.

questions.trap: The slice copies cost O(n) per level, which the merge already pays — so unlike sliced binary search, they leave the bound unchanged.

questions.vars: m, n = board dimensions, L = len(word)
code: if not (0 <= i < m and 0 <= j < n) or board[i][j] != word[k]:
found = (dfs(i + 1, j, k + 1) or dfs(i - 1, j, k + 1)
or dfs(i, j + 1, k + 1) or dfs(i, j - 1, k + 1))
return any(dfs(i, j, 0) for i in range(m) for j in range(n))

time.why: `m * n` start cells, and each `dfs` branches four ways for up to `L` levels → `4^L` per start.

space.why: The recursion is at most `L` frames deep; the board is marked in place with `#` and restored.

questions.why: The exponent is the *word* length, not the board size.
questions.trap: 3^L is the tighter bound (a step never goes straight back into the cell it came from) and grades correct too; 4^L is the usual answer.

questions.note: Time is for a single addNum call.

time.why: Each `addNum` does at most five heap pushes/pops, each `log n`.

space.why: Every number ever added stays in one of the two heaps.

questions.trap: Five heap operations are a constant factor, not a multiplier. And `findMedian` is O(1): it only peeks at the two roots.

time.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner `while` totals `n` pops over the whole run.

space.why: The stack can hold every index when the bars are strictly increasing.

questions.why: Amortised monotonic-stack argument: count pops over the whole run, not per outer step.
questions.trap: Being a Hard problem does not make it superlinear. Brute force is O(n^2); the stack removes the second factor.

time.why: The `x - 1 not in s` guard starts the `while` only at a run's first value, so each value is walked once overall.

space.why: `set(nums)` stores up to `n` distinct values.

questions.trap: The nested `while` reads as O(n^2), and is O(n^2) without the guard: every element of a long run would re-walk the run.

time.why: One pass over `nums`, with an O(1) average dict lookup per element.

space.why: `counts` gains an entry per distinct prefix sum, up to `n`.

questions.trap: The dict must count *how many times* each prefix sum occurred, not just whether it did — but that changes neither bound.

code: if not best or right - left < len(best):

time.why: `Counter(t)` is `m`; `right` and `left` each cross `s` once, so the inner `while` is amortised `n`.

space.why: `need[...] -= 1` adds a key for every distinct character of `s` too, so the counter holds up to `n + m` keys.

questions.why: `best` is the returned answer, so it does not count; on a fixed alphabet the counter is O(1).
questions.trap: The `while need[s[left]] < 0` loop never rewinds `left`, so it is amortised O(n) over the whole run, not O(n) per step.

questions.title: Building a string with +=

time.why: Each `out += ch` copies the whole string so far: `1 + 2 + … + n` → `n²` character copies.

space.why: Building the new string keeps an `O(n)` copy alive beside the old one.

questions.why: Strings are immutable; `"".join(chars)` is the O(n) version.
questions.trap: CPython's in-place resize can make this look linear, but it is an unguaranteed implementation detail. In an interview say O(n^2), then offer `join`.

questions.title: `in` on a list, inside a loop

time.why: `for x in a` runs `n` times, and `x in b` on a list hides an `m`-step linear scan.

space.why: Only the `total` counter.

questions.trap: `in` on a set is O(1). `b = set(b)` before the loop gives O(n + m) time for O(m) space — the top one-line fix in Python interviews.

questions.title: Draining a list with pop(0)

time.why: `items.pop(0)` shifts every remaining element down a slot — `O(n)` per call, `n` calls → `n²`.

space.why: `out` is the returned list and `items` shrinks as it grows, so the extra memory is `O(1)`.

questions.why: The `O(n)` of `out` is the output; counting it is also accepted.
questions.trap: BFS uses `collections.deque` for this reason: `popleft()` is O(1), while `list.pop(0)` silently makes a traversal quadratic. `list.pop()` from the end is O(1).

questions.title: heapify, then pop k times
questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = how many to take

time.why: `heapify` is a bottom-up `O(n)`, then `k` × `heappop` at `log n` each.

space.why: `heapify` rearranges `nums` in place; the `k`-item list is the returned output.

questions.trap: Calling heapify O(n log n) is the classic overcount: most nodes sit near the leaves and barely sift, so the series sums to O(n).

questions.title: Nested loop starting at i + 1

time.why: `for j in range(i + 1, …)` runs `n-1, n-2, …, 1` times → `n(n-1)/2` → `n²`.

space.why: Two loop indices and a counter.

questions.trap: "It only does half the work" is true and irrelevant: halving is a constant factor, which Big-O drops.

questions.title: Loop whose work halves each round
